title: Training diary and measuring progress
summary: What to write in a training diary and how to see progress: scores, hit rates by target type, two short ratings and video.

body.html: Memory lets you down: in a month you will not remember which target was not working or what your coach advised. A training diary keeps this for you and shows how you are improving.

After each session, note the date, the ground, the weather and the light. Write how many targets you shot and how many you broke. Note which targets you worked on, for example a crosser from right to left or an incomer. Add what worked and what did not, your coach's main tip and your kit: choke, cartridges and lens.

Add two short ratings. First, how nervous or excited you felt, from 0 (completely calm) to 10 (very tense). After a few weeks you may see at which level you shoot well. Studies, mostly in other sports, suggest that this level differs from person to person. This probably applies to clay shooting too.

Second, tick your process goals: goals about what you do on each target, not about the score. Did you do your full pre-shot routine on each target? Did you reset after a miss, that is, let it go and start the next target fresh? Research on goal setting suggests that goals about what you do help more than goals about winning or finishing in a certain place. A personal score target, such as 22 out of 25, sits between the two: it is about the result, but only your own. The studies come mostly from other sports, but this probably applies to clay shooting too. More in Process goals and the score.
Write straight away, while it is fresh. A few lines in a notebook or on your phone are enough. What matters is doing it regularly and honestly: note the good days and the bad ones.

How to measure progress. The simplest measure is your score in a round. More useful is your hit rate by target type. You may see, for example, that crossers now break 70% of the time but incomers only 40%. Your weak spots show what to work on next.

Video helps a lot. Ask someone to film you from the side and from behind, from a safe spot and with the ground's permission. The footage shows whether your head lifts off the stock and whether the mount is the same each time. It also shows whether you stop the gun: the barrels freeze at the moment you fire instead of moving on with the target. Watch it with your coach. Keep other people out of the frame unless they agree.

Do not expect a straight line. Many coaches see progress in shooting come in steps: weeks on one level, then a clear jump. Compare yourself with yourself a month ago, not with others. Once you compete, your results and accuracy in your ClayArena shooter profile become one more record (What the numbers in a profile mean).

notes.html: Filming a junior needs the parents' consent and the ground's permission. Keep such videos private and share them only with the coach.

key_points.html: A diary keeps your coach's tips and shows how you are improving
Note the targets, score, tips, kit and how you felt
Rate your nerves from 0 to 10 and tick your process goals
Hit rate by target type and video show what to work on
Progress often comes in steps, so compare yourself with yourself

did_you_know.html: Many shooters keep a diary for years and reread what worked last time before going back to a familiar ground.

quiz.q: What shows most clearly which targets to work on?

options.text: The total number of shots fired
Your hit rate by target type

quiz.explain: It shows which targets go worse than others.

quiz.q: Why rate your nerves from 0 to 10 after a session or a round?

options.text: To find the level at which you shoot well
To show the referee that you are ready
Because the FITASC rules ask for it

quiz.explain: The level at which people perform well differs from person to person; notes over a few weeks help you find yours.

quiz.q: What can a video of your shooting show?

options.text: The exact speed of the target in km/h
Nothing that a coach could really use
Whether your head lifts and the gun stops

quiz.explain: Video shows faults you cannot feel during the shot.
